text.p: Great Western Financial Corp is likely to contact a number of other financial institutions about a possible merger, but few can provide the cost savings hostile suitor H.F. Ahmanson can offer.
"It's the ultimate hand-in-glove merger due to the dramatic overlap, cost savings and synergies," said Charlotte Chamberlain, analyst with Jefferies and Co.
Even so, Chamberlain and others expect a bidding war to emerge as Ahmanson's $6.3 billion bid put in play a valuable property in the consolidating California thrift market.

"You're looking at a market with not a lot of sizeable acquisitions left," said Lloyd Greif of Greif & Co. "The fact that Ahmanson made an unsolicited bid after previous talks had failed indicates it perceived there's not a lot of time."
On Monday night, Ahmanson offered to swap 1.05 of its shares for each Great Western share, valuing Great Western at about $45.15 a share based on Wednesday's share price.

"We've not seen the end of the bidding by any stretch of the imagination," said Jeff Naschek of Salomon Brothers, who believes Washington Mutual Inc could bid as high as 0.9 of its shares, or about $50 a share, for Great Western.
"I think Washington Mutual could bid that high and still show earnings accretion," Naschek said. "For that matter, I think Ahmanson still has room to go on its bid."
Seattle-based Washington Mutual, which recently acquired Keystone Holdings Inc and Keystone's American Savings Bank unit, declined comment.
Ahmanson Chief Executive Charles Rinehart on Tuesday said he believed Ahmanson's offer was compelling, but he did not rule out raising the bid.
Great Western added nothing Wednesday to its statement on Tuesday that it was reviewing the offer.

"The single most obvious rival bidder is Washington Mutual since they've been explicit about their desire to expand in California. But its uncertain if it can match Ahmanson," said David Berry, analyst with Keefe Bruyette Woods.
Minneapolis-based First Bank System Inc, which lost a bitter battle against Wells Fargo and Co for First Interstate, may also return to the California fray.
First Bank System declined comment as did other potential suitors Norwest Corp and NationsBank Corp.
"If I was a director of Great Western, I'd feel duty bound to get a higher bid on the table," said Greif.
Great Western's shares dipped 1/8 to 44-3/4, and Ahmanson's shares fell 2 to 42-7/8.
"The stocks are trading in a way that is suggesting a third party might emerge," said one takeover specialist.
Several analysts believe Ahmanson would find itself on the block if it fail to acquire Great Western. "If Ahmanson is unsuccessful, Ahmanson itself is in play," said Greif.
Furthermore, several analysts said a combined Ahmanson-Great Western entity would not be immune to acquisitive banks seeking a foothold in California.
